# A complete plant breeding programme, and what it costs in diversity {#sec-programme}



The seventh consequence for the pipeline drawn in @sec-plant-literature is to
report the diversity cost per cycle explicitly whenever cycles are shortened.
This chapter measures that cost in a whole programme, but as a **stock**: the
change in gene diversity after 15 years, for arms whose cycle lengths in years
it also states. It does not report a rate per cycle, because the cycles of the
programme overlap (@sec-programme-assumptions).

@sec-alphasimr, built back in the Simulation part, assembled AlphaSimR's
primitives into a *hybrid* scheme: two
heterotic pools, reciprocal testers, a commercial cross at the end. This chapter
assembles the same primitives into the other kind of programme -- an
**inbred-line** pipeline, where the product is a variety rather than a hybrid,
and where the organising problem is not which cross to sell but how many
genotypes to carry through how many stages of field testing.

The scheme is the staged wheat programme of @gaynor2017, as reduced for the
AlphaSimR course vignette (@gorjanc2022, week 5 C) and reduced further here
(the configuration, and how it differs from both, is stated in @sec-programme-scheme). It is a
stylised inbred-line programme, not a survey of programmes in use. It is worth
building because it exposes something the hybrid chapter
cannot: **the trade between the number of genotypes tested and the precision
with which each is measured.** A breeder has a fixed number of plots. Spending
them on more entries scored once or fewer entries scored with eight replicates
(the course calls replicates "locations"; they are not locations here, see
@sec-programme-reps) is the same budget spent two ways, and the staged trial is
the standard compromise.
This chapter sets that trade up but does not measure it: it never varies the
number of entries against the replication at a fixed number of plots. The
Mating and testing design part measures allocation of plots between crosses and
locations, for hybrids, in @sec-mating, @sec-sparse and @sec-joint; none of
those chapters is a measurement on this inbred-line programme.

Then the chapter does what the course vignette does not (it reports the genetic
mean and variance only): it puts the book's diversity machinery over the result,
and asks what the faster programme spends to be faster.

## The scheme {#sec-programme-scheme}

The configuration. It is the author's own reduction, not the course's and not
Gaynor et al.'s. Gaynor et al. (Table 1 and the Methods, pp. 2375-2377) start
from 50 founders and run 100 crosses a year, 100 doubled-haploid (DH) lines per
cross, 10,000 headrows, 500 lines in the preliminary trial, 50 in the advanced
trial and 10 in the elite trial. The course vignette reduces that to 30
founders on 21 chromosomes, 30 crosses, 50 DH lines per cross (1500 headrows),
at most 10 lines per cross into the preliminary trial and 300, 25 and 5 entries
in the three trials, with 50 causal sites (quantitative trait loci, QTL) per chromosome. The values below
(`sch`) reduce it again; @fig-programme-stages draws the stages.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sch <- list(
  n_founders = 40, n_chr = 10, n_qtl = 60,   # founder genomes
  n_neutral = 0,                             # neutral sites per chromosome (0 = every site is a QTL)
  n_crosses  = 20, n_dh = 20, fam_max = 5,   # crossing and DH production
  n_pyt = 60, n_ayt = 12, n_eyt = 4,         # entries per yield trial
  rep_hdrw = 1/4, rep_pyt = 1, rep_ayt = 4, rep_eyt = 8,   # replicates per stage
  var_e = 0.4, gs_boost = 3, n_burn = 7, n_years = 15,
  gs_from = 6                                # first year a genomic arm switches on
)
n_hdrw <- sch$n_crosses * sch$n_dh           # every DH line is scored in the headrows
fx <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf("%.*f", d, x)   # fixed decimals for inline numbers
n_probe <- 48                                # seeds of the neutral-locus probe
```
:::

Seven stages (@fig-programme-stages), and the logic connecting them is a single
idea: **at every step, entries fall and replication rises.**
400 doubled-haploid lines
are scored once, cheaply, in unreplicated headrows; 60 survive into a
preliminary yield trial (PYT) with 1 replicate; 12 into an
advanced trial (AYT) with 4; 4 into an
elite trial (EYT) with 8. The number of entries falls by factors of
6.7, 5.0 and
3.0 over the three steps, not by a constant factor.

`rep_hdrw = 1/4` is the course's device for a stage *less* precise than a single
plot: headrows are scored visually on a short row, which carries less
information than one replicated plot, so the plot-error variance is multiplied by
four. `fam_max` caps how many DH lines any one cross may contribute to the
preliminary trial -- `selectWithinFam()` from @sec-alphasimr's Step 6, holding
the genetic base open against a truncation that would otherwise take the whole
trial from the two best crosses.

### What `reps` does, and what it does not {#sec-programme-reps}

`reps` in `setPheno()` is the argument @sec-alphasimr's Step 2 flagged as the
plant idiom, and the course calls its values "locations". It divides the
**plot-error variance** `varE` by the number of replicates and nothing else. The
genotype-by-environment (GxE) term enters a phenotype differently. In AlphaSimR
2.1.0 the trait of `addTraitAG(varGxE = )` gives each entry a deviate
$g_i$ of variance `varGxE`, and a `setPheno()` call multiplies every $g_i$ by
**one** standard-normal draw $z$ made for that call and shared by all entries of
the call; `reps` does not average it. The chunk checks that structure by its
consequence, in two parts. With `varE = 0`, the departures of the phenotypes
from the genetic values over four calls (two with `reps = 1`, two with
`reps = 8`) are one vector scaled four times, so the matrix has rank one: one
shared deviate per call. That check is blind to a rescaling of each call, so it
cannot say whether `reps` divides the GxE term; the second part measures it
directly, as the mean squared departure over 2000 calls at `reps = 1` and at
`reps = 8`, which would fall eight-fold at `reps = 8` if `reps` averaged GxE.
The chunk then measures the accuracy of
an entry mean (@tbl-programme-accuracy), $r = \text{cor}(\text{genetic value}, \text{phenotype})$ over the
40 founders, as the number of replicates grows, with and without the GxE term.


::: {#tbl-programme-accuracy .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Accuracy of an entry mean, cor(genetic value, phenotype) over the 40 founder lines of seed 7 (`quickHaplo()`, 10 x 60 QTL, `var` = 0.1, `varE` = 0.4), by number of replicates `reps`, with the GxE variance of the chapter (`varGxE` = 0.2) and with none. Mean and standard deviation over 300 `setPheno()` calls per cell, seed 11 before each cell; the 0.25 row is the headrows, 1 the PYT, 3 the surrogate genomic value `gs_boost`, 4 the AYT, 8 the EYT. Dimensionless, three decimals.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(7)
fg_acc <- quickHaplo(nInd = 40, nChr = 10, segSites = 60, inbred = TRUE)
mk <- function(vg) {
  SP <- SimParam$new(fg_acc)
  SP$addTraitAG(nQtlPerChr = 60, mean = 4, var = 0.1, varGxE = vg)
  list(SP = SP, pop = newPop(fg_acc, simParam = SP))
}
# GxE enters as g_i * z, one z per call: varE = 0 leaves a rank-one residual matrix
m <- mk(0.2)
res <- sapply(c(1, 1, 8, 8), function(r)
  setPheno(m$pop, varE = 0, reps = r, onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = m$SP)[, 1] -
    gv(m$pop)[, 1])
sv <- svd(res)[["d"]]
stopifnot(sv[2] < 1e-8 * sv[1])
set.seed(5)
msq <- sapply(c(1, 8), function(r) mean(replicate(2000,
  (setPheno(m$pop, varE = 0, reps = r, onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = m$SP)[, 1] -
     gv(m$pop)[, 1])^2)))
stopifnot(msq[2] / msq[1] > 0.5)          # eight-fold division would give 0.125
acc <- function(vg, r, seed = 11) {
  m <- mk(vg); set.seed(seed)
  a <- replicate(300, cor(gv(m$pop)[, 1],
                          setPheno(m$pop, varE = sch$var_e, reps = r,
                                   onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = m$SP)[, 1]))
  c(mean(a), stats::sd(a))
}
reps_grid <- c(0.25, 1, 3, 4, 8)
tab_acc <- t(sapply(reps_grid, function(r) c(acc(0.2, r), acc(0, r))))
dimnames(tab_acc) <- list(reps = reps_grid,
  c("GxE mean", "GxE sd", "no GxE mean", "no GxE sd"))
varG_found <- stats::var(gv(m$pop)[, 1])
fmt(tab_acc, 3)
```

The mean squared departure of the phenotype from the genetic value, with
`varE = 0`, is 0.202 at `reps = 1` and 0.200 at
`reps = 8`, against `varGxE` = 0.2: `reps` does not divide the GxE term (it
would give 0.025 at 8 if it did). The founders' additive variance is 0.103 (`var = 0.1`), so the
GxE variance of 0.2 is about twice it. Eight replicates raise the accuracy of an
entry mean from 0.40 to 0.63 with the
GxE term, against 0.45 to 0.82 without it, and the
standard deviation across calls stays at 0.18 where the
GxE term is present against 0.04 where it is not.
Selection accuracy at the last stage is higher
because the plot-error variance has been divided by eight, not because the trait
became more heritable; but it is bounded by a GxE term that replication does not
reduce and that changes from call to call. What the chapter exposes is therefore the trade
between entries and plot-error precision under one shared, random environmental
shift per `setPheno()` call, and not between entries and independent
locations. The printed `acc_pyt` of the runs below is
`cor(gv, phenotype)` of the PYT at one replicate (the row `1` of
@tbl-programme-accuracy, one call per year), whichever arm is run.

## Why a breeding programme needs a burn-in

The loop below advances every stage by one year, simultaneously. That only means
something if all seven stages are already *occupied*, by cohorts of different
ages: this year's elite trial was crossed five years before this year's crossing
block (the cohort in the DH stage was crossed one year before it, the headrows
two, the PYT three, the AYT four, the EYT five). Starting the loop from an empty programme would
compare a year-1 elite trial that does not exist against a year-1 headrow that
does.

The fix is the staggered fill in the course's vignette, and it is the most
confusing seven lines in it:

```r
for (year in 1:7) {
  F1 <- randCross(Parents, n_crosses)
  if (year < 7) DH   <- makeDH(F1, n_dh)
  if (year < 6) HDRW <- setPheno(DH, reps = rep_hdrw)
  if (year < 5) PYT  <- ...
  if (year < 4) AYT  <- ...
  if (year < 3) EYT  <- ...
}
```

Read it as a triangle rather than a loop. On the first pass every stage runs, so
every stage holds a cohort. On the third pass the elite trial is skipped (it runs
on the first two only), so the cohort sitting in it is older than the one behind
it; the advanced trial is skipped from the fourth pass, the preliminary trial
from the fifth, the headrows from the sixth and the DH production from the
seventh. By the seventh pass only the crossing block still runs. What comes out
is a programme in which each stage holds a cohort of the right age relative to
its neighbours -- a
*steady state*, which is the only state in which a per-year genetic gain is a
meaningful number. (The function below writes the thresholds as offsets of
`n_burn`, which gives the same thresholds, 7 down to 3, at `n_burn = 7`.)

## One programme, fifteen years

The whole scheme is one function. It is written out rather than packaged
because the loop is the thing being taught, and because a reader adapting it to
their own programme will edit the loop, not call it. Its argument `arm` selects
one of five programmes, all sharing the burn-in and the stage sizes of `sch`:

- `"ps"`, the **phenotypic** programme: selection on phenotype throughout;
  parents are all `n_eyt + n_ayt` lines of the EYT and the AYT, so there is no
  truncation at the parents' step.
- `"l1"`, **lever 1 alone**: from year `gs_from`, the PYT-to-AYT step uses a
  surrogate genomic value; parents as in `"ps"`.
- `"l2"`, **lever 2 alone**: from year `gs_from`, parents are the best
  `n_eyt + n_ayt` of the `n_eyt + n_ayt + n_pyt` lines of EYT, AYT and PYT by
  the surrogate genomic value (raw phenotype for the EYT and AYT lines, the
  surrogate for the PYT lines); the PYT-to-AYT step is phenotypic.
- `"gs"`, **both levers**.
- `"ctl"`, a **control** for lever 2: parents are the best `n_eyt + n_ayt` of
  the same `n_eyt + n_ayt + n_pyt` lines, truncated by plain phenotype, with no
  surrogate anywhere.

The surrogate genomic value is a phenotype of the same line simulated at
`gs_boost` times the PYT replication, in a separate `setPheno()` call; its
accuracy is the row `3` of @tbl-programme-accuracy (0.54
with GxE, 0.66 without), and it is a phenotypic
correlation, not a prediction accuracy fitted from markers. In `"l2"` and
`"ctl"` the candidates come from different cohorts and different `setPheno()`
calls, so the selection criterion compares lines measured with unequal
precision and under different GxE deviates; this is part of what the arms do,
and the control inherits it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
gd_of <- function(pop, SP, loci = c("qtl", "neutral")) {
  loci <- match.arg(loci)
  g <- pullSegSiteGeno(pop, simParam = SP)
  is_q <- colnames(g) %in% colnames(pullQtlGeno(pop, simParam = SP))
  1 - mean(molecular_coancestry(
    g[, if (loci == "qtl") is_q else !is_q, drop = FALSE] / 2))
}

run_programme <- function(cfg, seed, arm = c("ps", "l1", "l2", "gs", "ctl")) {
  arm <- match.arg(arm)
  lever1 <- arm %in% c("l1", "gs")   # surrogate genomic value for PYT -> AYT
  lever2 <- arm %in% c("l2", "gs")   # parents from c(EYT, AYT, PYT)
  stopifnot(cfg$n_burn >= 7)
  # founders: re-drawn per arm from the same seed (quickHaplo() is deterministic)
  set.seed(seed)
  fg <- quickHaplo(nInd = cfg$n_founders, nChr = cfg$n_chr,
                   segSites = cfg$n_qtl + cfg$n_neutral, inbred = TRUE)
  SP <- SimParam$new(fg)
  SP$addTraitAG(nQtlPerChr = cfg$n_qtl, mean = 4, var = 0.1, varGxE = 0.2)
  ph <- function(p, r) setPheno(p, varE = cfg$var_e, reps = r, simParam = SP)

  # --- burn-in: fill every stage with a cohort of the right age ---
  Parents <- newPop(fg, simParam = SP)
  gd_founders <- gd_of(Parents, SP)
  nb <- cfg$n_burn
  for (year in 1:nb) {
    F1 <- randCross(Parents, cfg$n_crosses, simParam = SP)
    if (year < nb)     DH   <- makeDH(F1, cfg$n_dh, simParam = SP)
    if (year < nb - 1) HDRW <- ph(DH, cfg$rep_hdrw)
    if (year < nb - 2) {
      PYT <- selectWithinFam(HDRW, nInd = cfg$fam_max, use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
      PYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_pyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_pyt)
    }
    if (year < nb - 3)
      AYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_ayt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_ayt)
    if (year < nb - 4)
      EYT <- ph(selectInd(AYT, nInd = cfg$n_eyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_eyt)
  }

  # --- advancing years, last stage first so each reads the previous cohort ---
  out <- data.frame(year = 1:cfg$n_years, meanG = NA_real_, varG = NA_real_,
                    acc_pyt = NA_real_, gd_pyt = NA_real_, gd_parents = NA_real_,
                    gd_pyt_neutral = NA_real_, par_eyt = NA_integer_,
                    par_ayt = NA_integer_, par_pyt = NA_integer_)
  for (year in 1:cfg$n_years) {
    on <- year >= cfg$gs_from          # the switch of the arm is on from this year

    # (the released variety, the best EYT entry, is not tracked: the chapter
    #  measures the pipeline, not the released line)
    EYT <- ph(selectInd(AYT, nInd = cfg$n_eyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
              cfg$rep_eyt)

    if (lever1 && on) {  # lever 1: a more accurate criterion at the PYT stage
      PYT@ebv <- setPheno(PYT, varE = cfg$var_e,
                          reps = cfg$rep_pyt * cfg$gs_boost,
                          onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = SP)
      AYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_ayt, use = "ebv", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_ayt)
    } else {
      AYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_ayt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
                cfg$rep_ayt)
    }

    PYT <- selectWithinFam(HDRW, nInd = cfg$fam_max, use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
    PYT <- ph(selectInd(PYT, nInd = cfg$n_pyt, use = "pheno", simParam = SP),
              cfg$rep_pyt)
    HDRW <- ph(DH, cfg$rep_hdrw)
    DH   <- makeDH(F1, cfg$n_dh, simParam = SP)

    if (lever2 && on) {  # lever 2: recycle parents a year earlier, from the PYT
      PYT@ebv <- setPheno(PYT, varE = cfg$var_e,
                          reps = cfg$rep_pyt * cfg$gs_boost,
                          onlyPheno = TRUE, simParam = SP)
      EYT@ebv <- pheno(EYT); AYT@ebv <- pheno(AYT)
      Parents <- selectInd(c(EYT, AYT, PYT), nInd = cfg$n_eyt + cfg$n_ayt,
                           use = "ebv", simParam = SP)
    } else if (arm == "ctl" && on) {   # control: the same wider set, plain phenotype
      Parents <- selectInd(c(EYT, AYT, PYT), nInd = cfg$n_eyt + cfg$n_ayt,
                           use = "pheno", simParam = SP)
    } else {
      Parents <- c(EYT, AYT)
    }
    F1 <- randCross(Parents, cfg$n_crosses, simParam = SP)

    out$meanG[year]      <- meanG(PYT)
    out$varG[year]       <- varG(PYT)
    out$acc_pyt[year]    <- stats::cor(PYT@gv[, 1], PYT@pheno[, 1])
    out$gd_pyt[year]     <- gd_of(PYT, SP)
    out$gd_parents[year] <- gd_of(Parents, SP)
    if (cfg$n_neutral > 0) out$gd_pyt_neutral[year] <- gd_of(PYT, SP, "neutral")
    out$par_eyt[year] <- sum(Parents@id %in% EYT@id)
    out$par_ayt[year] <- sum(Parents@id %in% AYT@id)
    out$par_pyt[year] <- sum(Parents@id %in% PYT@id)
  }
  out$gd_founders <- gd_founders
  out
}
```
:::


Two details are worth pausing on.

**The advancing loop runs backwards.** The elite trial is filled *before* the
advanced trial is refilled, which is before the preliminary trial is refilled.
Written in the other order, `EYT` would be selected from an `AYT` that had
already been overwritten with this year's cohort, and the programme would
advance two stages per year without anyone noticing. Ordering is the whole
correctness argument of a staged simulation.

**Progress is reported at the PYT.** It is the first stage with a yield
phenotype and the last with enough entries for a variance to mean anything --
`meanG` on four elite lines is noise. This is the course's choice and it is the
right one.

The phenotypic arm on seed 1 is the first run (@tbl-programme-seed1-ps).

## These numbers are reproducible

The founders come from `quickHaplo()`, which is seeded by `set.seed()`, so
`run_programme(sch, seed = 1)` returns the same data frame every time -- unlike
@sec-alphasimr's Step 8, whose `runMacs2()` founders are not reproducible.
That is what makes the paired comparison below legitimate: the phenotypic and
genomic arms are run from the *same* seed, so they share founders, and every
difference between them is attributable to the scheme.

This is a documented exception to rule 1 of @sec-alphasimr's Step 1 (found the
founders once and branch every arm off that object): each arm here re-draws its
founders from the same seed. It is safe only because `quickHaplo()` is plain R
sampling; the design chunk below asserts, for every seed, that years 1 to 5
(burn-in and the years before the arms differ) are identical across the five
arms, which they could not be if the founders differed.
:::

## Genomic selection: two levers, separated {#sec-programme-levers}

Genomic selection is usually described as buying accuracy. In a staged
programme it can buy two things, and the arms above have a switch for each:

1. **Accuracy earlier in the cycle (lever 1).** A prediction is available on a
   line that has been genotyped but barely phenotyped, so the advance from
   preliminary to advanced trial can be made on better information than one
   replicate of yield.
2. **A shorter generation interval (lever 2).** Parents can be recycled from the
   preliminary trial instead of waiting for the elite trial. Define the cycle
   length $T$ of a parent as the years from the crossing that produced its
   cohort to the crossing that uses it. By the loop above a cross in year $t$
   gives DH lines in year $t+1$, headrows in $t+2$, the PYT in $t+3$, the AYT in
   $t+4$ and the EYT in $t+5$, and the parents are chosen in the year their
   cohort is in the trial: $T = 3$, $4$, $5$ years for a parent taken from the
   PYT, the AYT and the EYT.

The breeder's equation of @sec-response, $R = i\,r\,\sigma_A$
(@eq-response-breeders), is the response to **one round** of selection: $i$ the
intensity, $r$ the accuracy and $\sigma_A$ the additive standard deviation. A
response per year is that response divided by the years $T$ a round takes. That
division is the chapter's own bookkeeping, not an equation of @sec-response, and
it assumes discrete rounds of a common length (assumption A4 of
@sec-genomic-era), which this overlapping programme, with parents of three
different lengths, only approximates. It is used below to read a direction, not
to predict a number.

Two statements in the literature are about these levers, and neither transfers
as a ratio. @gaynor2017 report, in their simulations, that a genomic programme
that changes accuracy only gained 1.21 (95 % confidence interval, CI, 1.18-1.25) to 1.39 times the
gain of the conventional programme, and the two-part programmes, which also
shorten the cycle, 2.36 to 2.47 times (p. 2379; the ranges span their
genotype-by-year variance settings, 0 and 10); they write that in the
two-part programmes "the shortening of breeding cycle time was the major driver
of increased genetic gain" (p. 2381). Their genomic programmes are
cost-matched (fewer DH lines per cross to pay for genotyping, Table 1),
whereas the genomic arms here are free. And
@meuwissen2001 state in their abstract that marker-based selection could
substantially increase the rate of genetic gain, especially if combined with
reproductive techniques that shorten the generation interval (the full text was
not consulted for this chapter). That the second lever is the larger is thus
reported for one simulated design; what follows measures it for this one.

This chapter mimics the prediction rather than fitting one: `ebv` is filled with
a phenotype simulated at `gs_boost` times the replication, which is a stand-in
for a genomic prediction of the corresponding accuracy. @sec-genomic-prediction
is where the book actually fits prediction models and measures what accuracy is
attainable; the honest statement here is that this chapter *assumes* an accuracy
(`gs_boost = 3`, the row `3` of @tbl-programme-accuracy) and studies its
consequences, rather than earning it.

## The comparison, replicated {#sec-programme-comparison}

One run of one seed is an anecdote. Five arms are cheap enough to replicate.
The design runs all five arms on 120 seeds (600 programme runs, several minutes
to execute); the seeds are read in five batches of 24, because 24 seeds is a size a single
experiment of this kind can easily have and the batches show how far such an
experiment moves.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(meanG ~ year,

per_seed <- function(f) sapply(runs, function(r) vapply(r, f, numeric(1)))
S <- list(
  gain   = per_seed(rate),
  gd_pyt = per_seed(function(d) d[["gd_pyt"]][last]),
  gd_par = per_seed(function(d) d[["gd_parents"]][last]),
  par_eyt = per_seed(function(d) mean(d[["par_eyt"]][d$year >= sch$gs_from])),

}

}))

**Gain.** The phenotypic arm gains 0.0575 (0.0013) per year (mean and
s.e.). Relative to it, lever 1 alone adds 0.0086
(t = 7.2), lever 2 alone 0.0267
(t = 21.3) and both levers 0.0294
(t = 21.1); the ratio of the mean rates, both levers
over phenotypic, is
1.51 (95 % bootstrap
interval over seeds, 1.46 to 1.56). The two single
effects add to 0.0353, more
than the joint 0.0294, and adding lever 1 to lever 2 gives
0.0027 (t = 2.0). In this
simulation, therefore, lever 2 contributes the larger part of the gain and
lever 1 adds little once lever 2 is on. That is one configuration, with an
assumed surrogate accuracy; it does not show that the second lever is
normally the larger. Nor is it a statement about lever 1 in general: the PYT
genetic mean that measures the gain is a lagged readout of a selection made
one stage later, so lever 1 shows in it only through the parents.



The control recycles parents from the same wider set, but by plain phenotype. It
gains 0.0184 per year over the phenotypic arm
(t = 15.8), which is
69 % of lever 2's
gain, and differs from lever 2 alone by -0.0083
(t = -6.4). The mean cycle lengths $T$ of
@tbl-programme-arms are 4.25 years for the
phenotypic arm, 3.34 for lever 2 alone and
3.26 for the control. If $i\,r\,\sigma_A$ per round were unchanged, the gain per year would scale as $1/T$,
by the ratio 1.27 for
lever 2 alone and 1.30 for the
control; the observed ratios of mean gains are
1.46 (95 % bootstrap
interval over seeds, 1.42 to 1.51) and
1.32
(1.28 to 1.36). Lever 2's ratio exceeds the ratio of cycle lengths by
0.19 (95 % interval, one resample of seeds for gains and cycle
lengths, 0.14 to 0.24), an interval that excludes zero; the control's exceeds it
by 0.017 (-0.025 to 0.059), an interval that includes zero. The
control's ratio is therefore of the size of the shortening of the cycle, within this
resolution; lever 2's is larger. This is
consistent with the surrogate genomic value in the parent choice adding to the
accuracy $r$ or the intensity $i$ beyond what the shorter cycle gives, but
neither $i$ nor $r$ is measured per round here, the rates are averages over a
transient, and $T$ is a mean of three parent sources; it is a reading, not a
decomposition. The premise itself is a reference point, not a description of
either arm: lever 2 and the control also change the intensity at the parent
step, which takes the best 16 of
76 lines instead of all
16.

**Which lever carries the loss.** Lever 1 alone changes the PYT gene diversity
at year 15 by -0.0035 (t = -1.3) and
that of the parent set by -0.0124
(t = -4.9). Lever 2 alone changes them by
-0.0242 (t = -6.5) and
-0.0220 (t = -6.5). The control, with no
genomic information at all, changes them by -0.0233
(t = -6.6) and -0.0286
(t = -7.9); against lever 2 alone the control differs by
0.0009 in the PYT (t = 0.2) and by
-0.0066 in the parent set (t = -1.6).
The year-15 loss of PYT diversity that goes with lever 2 is thus reproduced,
within the resolution of 120 seeds (the standard error of the
control-minus-lever-2 difference in the PYT is 0.0040), by
truncating the same wider candidate set on plain phenotype. It does not need a
genomic value. What it goes
with is a different parent step: the phenotypic arm takes all
16 lines of the EYT and the AYT as parents, with no
truncation, whereas the lever-2 arms and the control take the best
16 of 76, and
11.7 of them (lever 2) or
12.7 (control) come from the PYT. Lever 1 alone, whose parents are chosen as in the phenotypic arm,
lowers the diversity of the parent set but its effect on the PYT is not
resolved at this number of seeds; that is a statement about resolution, not
about absence.

What was not measured is why. A natural hypothesis is that parents truncated from
a wider set, and taken from a preliminary trial in which full sibs have not yet
been separated by later trials, are more closely related to each other, and that a shorter interval
accumulates coancestry faster per unit of time. This chapter does not test
it: it records the gene diversity of the parent set, not the coancestry among the
chosen parents, nor their family structure. @gaynor2017 give a different
mechanism for the loss of genetic *variance* under genomic selection: the Bulmer
effect of the increased selection accuracy in early stages, with effective
population size, selection intensity, accuracy and the number of cycles per year
as the factors of later changes (p. 2383). They name optimal contribution
selection, with introgression, as an established remedy for the decline of
genetic variance (p. 2382). That concerns variance, not molecular gene
diversity, and supports the direction, not this mechanism.

## The diversity ledger {#sec-programme-ledger}

The measurement above used gene diversity of the preliminary trial. The parent
set is the population that actually transmits, and it is the one an optimal
contribution scheme would act on. @tbl-programme-ledger gives both for the two
extreme arms, averaged over the 120 seeds.


::: {#tbl-programme-ledger .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Gene diversity GD = 1 - theta (QTL loci) of the PYT (60 lines) and of the parent set (16 lines) in years 1, 5, 10 and 15, mean (standard error over seeds) of 120 paired seeds, phenotypic (ps) and both-levers (gs) arms. Dimensionless. The levels include the diagonal of the coancestry matrix (f_ii = 1 for DH lines), whose weight 1/n differs between the PYT and parent columns, so they are not on one scale: compare arms and years within a column, not the two sets; the diagonal-free comparison is @tbl-programme-loss.'}

## Gene diversity with the diagonal is not comparable across set sizes

These three levels are not on one scale: for fully homozygous lines the diagonal of $f$ is 1, so that

$$
\theta = \frac{1}{n} + \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{n}\Bigr)\theta_{\text{off}},
\qquad
GD = \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{n}\Bigr)GD_{\text{off}},
$$ {#eq-programme-gdoff}

where $\theta_{\text{off}}$ is the mean of
$f_{ij}$ over pairs of distinct lines and $GD_{\text{off}} = 1 - \theta_{\text{off}}$
is the gene diversity between distinct lines (@eq-programme-gdoff is checked in the chunk
above on a random matrix of homozygous lines). $GD_{\text{off}}$ does not carry the
weight $1/n$, which differs among $n$ = 40 (founders),
60 (PYT) and 16 (parents). On that scale the
founders are at 0.5000, the year-1 PYT at 0.4761 and the
year-1 parent set at 0.4731. A part of the diversity of the founders
has therefore gone before the first row of the table, by
0.027 for the parents on the $GD_{\text{off}}$ scale, not
by the 0.044 that the levels above
suggest, 0.017
of which is the difference in diagonal weight between $n$ = 40 and
$n$ = 16.
:::

The loss is reported against both bases
(@tbl-programme-loss), per seed, with the standard error over seeds.

These numbers are **not** the quantity the book calls $\alpha$. The $\alpha$ of
@eq-catalogue-alpha (@sec-baseline) is $(GD_{\text{ref}} - GD_S)/GD_{\text{ref}}$,

the selected set, so that $\alpha = 0$ is a random sample and $\alpha < 0$ is possible. The
quantity in @tbl-programme-loss is the cumulative relative change over fifteen
years of one population against its own earlier value (year 1, or the founders):
there is no reference distribution of random subsets, it includes whatever drift
and burn-in do to a set of that size, and it can be compared with an $\alpha$
budget of @sec-ocs or @sec-combinatorial only as a different kind of number. I call

numerator and the denominator are gene diversities of sets of the same size, so the

## Status number, and why it is not the headline here

`status_number()` on a set of lines returns $N_s = 1/(2\theta)$. At biallelic
loci the group coancestry satisfies $\theta \in [1/2, 1]$, so
$N_s \in [1/2, 1]$ for *every* set of lines, whatever its size (@sec-ns,
@sec-sizing): $N_s$ is a monotone rescaling of $\theta$, not a head count. Here
it ranges over 0.62-0.98 across all
arms, seeds, years and both sets. It carries no information that $GD$ does not,
compressed into $[1/2, 1]$, which is why the ledger is written in $GD$. The
diagonal of $f$ does *not* dominate the mean coancestry here: it is
3.1 % of $\theta$ at $n$ = 60 (year-1 PYT) and
11.2 % at $n$ = 16 (year-1 parents).
:::

### Selection or bottleneck?

All 600 segregating sites of the design are QTL (the
chunk above asserts it: `segSites` equals `nQtlPerChr`). The gene diversity of the
ledger is therefore measured at causal loci, which selection acts on directly, and
no neutral locus is measured in the main design. The chapter also has no
no-selection arm, so the loss in @tbl-programme-loss cannot be split into what
selection did and what a bottleneck of 16 parents and
20 crosses a year would have done anyway. (@sec-alphasimr's Step 8
builds a paired no-selection control for the hybrid programme; this chapter has none.)
One probe bears on the question. It re-runs the phenotypic and the both-levers
arms on 48 seeds with 60 neutral sites added per chromosome beside the QTL
(`n_neutral = 60`, so `segSites` = 120 and the founders differ from the main
design), and measures the relative loss against year 1 at the QTL loci and at the
neutral loci separately (@tbl-programme-neutral).

At neutral loci the phenotypic arm loses 97 % (95 % bootstrap interval over seeds, 95-99 %) of what it loses at the QTL loci
and the both-levers arm 95 % (95 % bootstrap interval over seeds, 93-96 %). The within-seed excess of the QTL loss over the
neutral loss is resolved in both arms (@tbl-programme-neutral: t = 2.9
for the phenotypic arm and 6.4 for the both-levers arm, beyond the
critical value 2.01), and larger in the faster arm
(t of the difference of the two excesses = 2.7). So the loss is
mostly, not entirely, shared with neutral loci: it is consistent with a loss that is
mainly a bottleneck effect plus a smaller part, resolved here, that is specific to the loci
selection acts on or to what is linked to them. It does not separate the two:
neutral loci here lie on the same ten chromosomes as the QTL, and loci linked to selected ones lose diversity with them, so the neutral loss is
not a drift-only measure; and the difference between the arms
is present at neutral loci too (0.036 against 0.044
at the QTL loci, in the relative loss), so the extra loss of the faster arm is
not confined to the causal loci either. A random-parent arm would separate selection from
bottleneck; it is not built here.

What would an $\alpha$ budget mean here? Not a constraint on which hybrids to
sell, as in @sec-combinatorial, but a constraint on **which parents to recycle**:
the same optimal-contribution problem of @sec-ocs, applied to the
`c(EYT, AYT, PYT)` candidate set that the lever-2 arms select from. The candidate
set is small, the coancestry matrix is cheap, and the choice being
constrained is annual. @sec-ocs and @sec-combinatorial were developed and tested
on hybrid candidates, @sec-cycles follows the trajectories of constrained and
unconstrained hybrid programmes forward, and @sec-limits tests whether the
cumulative gain can be forecast from the rate of inbreeding; none of this is tested on the inbred-line programme of this chapter, and the
application to line parents is a proposal.

## Assumptions {#sec-programme-assumptions}

**What this models.** Staged testing with replication rising across stages,
genotype-by-environment interaction as a variance component
(`SP$addTraitAG(varGxE = )`, here 0.2 against a founder additive variance of 0.1,
entering as one shared deviate per `setPheno()` call, as in @sec-programme-reps),
doubled-haploid line development, within-family caps, a steady-state programme
reached through a burn-in, one additive trait with no dominance (assumption A7 of
@sec-genomic-era), and two genomic-selection levers with a switch each, plus a
phenotype-only control for the second.

**What it does not.** Genomic prediction is *mimicked* by adding replication,
not fitted -- so the accuracy is assumed rather than earned (its value, under the
chapter's GxE, is in @tbl-programme-accuracy), and the training
population, its size, and its relationship to the selection candidates play no
role (@sec-genomic-prediction is where they do). There is one trait, so the
index questions of @sec-alphasimr's Step 7 do not arise. Locations differ only
through plot error and a shared GxE deviate per call: there is no correlated
environment structure, no year effect, and no location-by-year term, so a
"replicate" here is an independent draw of plot error only and not an independent
location (the GxE deviate is common to all entries of a call and is not averaged
by `reps`). Doubled-haploid production is
instantaneous and never fails. Founders come from `quickHaplo()`, so they carry
no linkage disequilibrium -- @sec-alphasimr's Step 1 measures what that costs
and argues it is the right trade for a chapter about response rather than about
marker-QTL association. Every segregating site is a QTL, so the marker panel is the
causal set and gene diversity is measured at causal loci; this is the limit
@sec-genomic-era (assumption A5) states. There is no no-selection or random-parent
arm, so selection and the bottleneck are not separated (the probe above is
suggestive only). The base against which loss is reported is the programme's year
1 (or the founders), not a frozen allele-frequency base (assumption A6) and not a
random-subset reference.

**Against the assumptions of @sec-genomic-era.** The chapter keeps A2 (fully
inbred lines, by DH) and A7 (no dominance). It leaves A1 (an allogamous crop and an
F1 hybrid product: the product here is a line) and A4 (discrete cycles: the cycles
overlap, a stage holds cohorts of five different ages, and the parents of one cycle
come from three stages, so the cycle length $T$ is a mean of 3, 4 and 5 years and
a per-cycle rate is not computed). The results of @sec-genomic-era and of the
hybrid chapters do not transfer to this chapter by that route, nor this chapter's to theirs.

**Rate window.** The gain per year is the slope over years 6 to 15, which
includes the years before a parent chosen by a genomic arm in year 6 reaches the
PYT (three years for a PYT parent): it averages a transient, with a lag that
differs between arms.

## Where this connects

@sec-alphasimr supplies every primitive this chapter uses and builds them into
the hybrid scheme instead; the two chapters are the same toolkit pointed at the
two kinds of programme. @sec-response states the breeder's equation for one round
of selection; the per-year form used here is the division by the cycle length
stated above. @sec-genomic-prediction is
where an accuracy of the kind this chapter assumes is measured, on a trait generated
from the markers the models see; there it is finite because of training size, noise
and the rank bound, not because of a marker-versus-QTL gap. This book does not
measure that gap, and @sec-genomic-era (assumption A5) states its collapse as a
limit. How many crosses, entries and locations to plant for a fixed number of
plots is the subject of @sec-mating, @sec-sparse and @sec-joint, for hybrids.

The diversity result belongs to the book's spine. @sec-cycles shows the same
tension -- faster response, faster erosion -- with the package's own simulator
over a longer horizon, for the hybrid programme; @sec-limits tests whether the cumulative gain can be
forecast from the rate of erosion (three budgets tested; the 15-cycle gain is
reached for one of them, in the five-draw mean) and what the
frequency-based metrics cannot see; @sec-ocs is the machinery for spending
the budget deliberately rather than discovering afterwards what was spent.
